before.approach: Start at the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead (~4,875 ft) on SR-20, 4.7 miles west of Washington Pass. Follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound as it switchbacks up through forest and into larch parkland to Cutthroat Pass (~6,600 ft, ~4.9 mi) — this stretch has only intermittent small streams, so top off water here, since little reliable water exists again until Snowy Lakes. From Cutthroat Pass the PCT contours below Cutthroat Peak's west flank to Granite Pass (~6,600 ft, roughly 6.5-7 mi from the trailhead); this pass holds snow into July/August, and when snow-covered it's steep and exposed enough that an ice axe (and comfort self-arresting) is warranted. Beyond Granite Pass the trail sidehills below Tower Mountain's west side, crosses a cliff-cut, blasted-out section, loses a bit of elevation, and climbs again to Methow Pass (~9 mi). Roughly 10 miles in, just past Methow Pass at about 6,300 ft, a climbers'/use path branches right (east) off the PCT and climbs ~0.5 mi and ~400 ft to the Snowy Lakes basin — Lower Snowy Lake (~6,600 ft) or Upper Snowy Lake (~6,700 ft) — the standard base camp, with reliable water and good tent sites; most parties backpack in and climb from camp rather than going car-to-car. From camp near Lower Snowy Lake, head cross-country south toward Tower Mountain on a climbers' path, then make a short but strenuous traverse across a talus field, aiming for a distinctive large reddish boulder partway across. Beyond the boulder, a ramp on the left side of a large cave (which cuts about 25 yards into the mountainside and makes a good wind-sheltered rest stop) leads up to the base of the main summit gully — from here the route follows ledges on the gully's right side, zigzagging back toward the gully-notch in the ridge and up broken rock to the summit. Total distance to the base of the gully runs roughly 10-11 miles one-way with about 2,800-3,000 ft of net elevation gain from the trailhead to camp (cumulative gain over the Cutthroat/Granite/Methow pass rollercoaster is closer to 4,200 ft). The gully itself is the route's main hazard: the rock is notoriously loose and rockfall-prone, so helmets are strongly recommended and parties should climb one at a time, staying right and moving efficiently through the narrowest sections.

approach_variants.name: Rainy Pass PCT over Cutthroat, Granite and Methow Passes to Snowy Lakes, then the reddish boulder and the cave
approach_variants.notes:

Follow the Pacific Crest Trail northbound as it switchbacks up through forest and into larch parkland to Cutthroat Pass at about 6,600 ft, roughly 4.9 miles. THIS STRETCH HAS ONLY INTERMITTENT SMALL STREAMS, SO TOP OFF AT THE PASS; there is little reliable water again until Snowy Lakes.

From Cutthroat Pass the PCT contours below Cutthroat Peak's west flank to Granite Pass at about 6,600 ft, roughly 6.5-7 miles in. Granite Pass holds snow into July or August and when snow-covered is steep and exposed enough to warrant an ice axe. Beyond it the trail sidehills below Tower Mountain's west side, crosses a cliff-cut blasted-out section, loses a little elevation and climbs again to Methow Pass at about 9 miles.

Roughly 10 miles in, just past Methow Pass at about 6,300 ft, a climbers' use path branches RIGHT, east, off the PCT and climbs about half a mile and 400 ft to the Snowy Lakes basin, the standard base camp with reliable water and good tent sites.

approach_variants.baseFinding:
THE APPROACH FROM CAMP HAS THREE MARKERS AND ALL THREE ARE OBJECTS YOU CAN PUT A HAND ON, WHICH IS RARE AND IS WHY THIS ROUTE IS UNUSUALLY FINDABLE IN CLOUD.

FIRST: from camp near Lower Snowy Lake, head cross-country SOUTH toward Tower Mountain on a climbers' path, then make a short but strenuous traverse across a TALUS FIELD, AIMING FOR A DISTINCTIVE LARGE REDDISH BOULDER PARTWAY ACROSS. A single big red block in a talus field.

SECOND: BEYOND THE BOULDER, A RAMP ON THE LEFT SIDE OF A LARGE CAVE. THE CAVE CUTS ABOUT 25 YARDS INTO THE MOUNTAINSIDE and makes a good wind-sheltered rest stop. A cave you can walk twenty-five yards into is not something you can mistake for anything else.

THIRD: that ramp leads UP TO THE BASE OF THE MAIN SUMMIT GULLY. That gully is the route.

SO THE ORDER IS: TALUS, RED BOULDER, CAVE, RAMP ON ITS LEFT, GULLY. If you have crossed the talus and found no red boulder, you are off the traverse line. If you have found the boulder but no cave, keep going.

FROM THE BASE OF THE GULLY the route follows LEDGES ON THE GULLY'S RIGHT SIDE, zigzagging back toward the gully-notch in the ridge and up broken rock to the summit. Right-hand ledges, not the gully bed.

THE GULLY IS THE MAIN HAZARD OF THE WHOLE OUTING AND THE RULE IS ABOUT SPACING RATHER THAN TECHNIQUE: the rock is notoriously loose and rockfall-prone, so helmets on and CLIMB ONE AT A TIME THROUGH THE NARROWEST SECTIONS, staying right and moving efficiently.

fitnessSpec.hiking: Long PCT-based approach (roughly 11-13 miles round trip with on the order of 4,000+ ft of elevation gain depending on trailhead used) either as a long single-push day or an overnight basecamp at Snowy Lakes
fitnessSpec.packWeight: Light day-climbing kit (~20-30 lb) if carrying a rope/rack for the summit gully and short technical section; heavier if backpacking in to camp at Snowy Lakes

partner_requirements.approachTime: Roughly 6-8 hours one-way via the PCT to the Snowy Lakes basin and up to the summit gully; many parties split this into an overnight at Snowy Lakes rather than a single push
requiredSkills: confident 3rd-4th class scrambling without a rope
loose-rock / choss management (route is described as having an incredibly loose summit gully)
route-finding on unmarked, cairn-dependent alpine terrain
basic snow travel/self-arrest for lingering early-season snow on the approach and gully
willingness to rope up for the short 5.4 crux section when conditions warrant
partner_requirements.experienceLevel: Intermediate alpine scrambler/climber comfortable with unroped Class 4 terrain and able to competently lead or follow short Class 5.4 moves; prior loose-rock alpine scrambling experience strongly preferred

access.fees: Northwest Forest Pass or America the Beautiful/interagency pass required at the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead self-pay station (Northwest Forest Pass day fee is about $5/vehicle).
access.notes: Not inside North Cascades National Park — this corridor is entirely Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District). No Mount Rainier-style climbing fee applies here.
access.rules: Leave No Trace; camp on durable/existing sites at Snowy Lakes. Campfires are prohibited above 5,000 ft in the adjoining Pasayten Wilderness, and Snowy Lakes camp (~6,700 ft) sits well above that line, so plan on a stove only.
access.permit: A free self-issue Wilderness permit (available at the trailhead kiosk) is required for overnight camping along this Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest corridor, including Snowy Lakes camp. This is separate from the PCT long-distance permit, which is only needed for continuous PCT thru-hikes of 500+ miles.
access.closures: SR-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes for winter between the Ross Dam trailhead (MP 134) and the Silver Star Mountain gate (MP 171), a span that includes both Rainy and Washington Passes - typically early December through mid-April/May.
access.seasonal: WA-20 (North Cascades Highway) closes gate-to-gate roughly early December–mid/late April; the entire Washington Pass corridor is car-inaccessible in winter.
access.landManager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest, Methow Valley Ranger District (24 West Chewuch Rd, Winthrop, WA; (509) 996-4000); the approach runs along the southern edge of the Pasayten Wilderness.
access.land_manager: Okanogan-Wenatchee National Forest (Methow Valley Ranger District)
access.parking_pass: Northwest Forest Pass required at Washington Pass Overlook, Blue Lake, and Cutthroat trailheads — $5/day or $30/annual (America the Beautiful pass also honored).

overnight_permit.where: A Northwest Forest Pass, an America the Beautiful pass, or a Recreation.gov day pass covers parking at the Rainy Pass PCT North trailhead; no permit paperwork is needed to camp anywhere along this stretch of the Pacific Crest Trail.

waypoints.name: Rainy Pass PCT Trailhead
waypoints.note: USFS trailhead on SR-20 at Rainy Pass; self-issue wilderness permit and Northwest Forest Pass required at the kiosk.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead sits on SR-20, the North Cascades Highway, at Rainy Pass, about 4.7 miles west of Washington Pass. That stretch of Highway 20 typically closes for the winter and reopens in May, so check that it's open before you drive up. At the trailhead kiosk, fill out a self-issue wilderness permit and display a Northwest Forest Pass.

waypoints.name: Cutthroat Pass
waypoints.note: PCT crests the pass here with the first open views north into the Pasayten; trail keeps traversing north instead of dropping.
waypoints.directions: Head north on the PCT from the parking area; the trail climbs gently at first, then switchbacks up through forest into open larch parkland to reach the pass. Water on this stretch is limited to a few small intermittent streams, so fill up at the last of them, because there is little reliable water again until the lakes.

waypoints.name: Granite Pass
waypoints.note: Second, lower saddle on the PCT past Cutthroat Pass; the climbers' route toward Tower Mountain leaves the maintained trail somewhere past here.
waypoints.directions: The trail stays high and contours north below Cutthroat Peak's west flank, losing a little elevation to reach this lower saddle. Snow can lie across the traverse into midsummer, and where it does the slope beneath the tread is steep and run out enough to justify an ice axe and the ability to self-arrest. Do not mistake this saddle for the pass behind you: the climbers' route toward Tower leaves the trail past here, not at the first pass.

waypoints.name: Snowy Lakes Trail spur
waypoints.note: Small, easy-to-miss unmarked spur leaves the PCT here for Snowy Lakes basin; gains ~500 ft over the final half mile to the lakes.
waypoints.directions: Beyond the pass the PCT sidehills below Tower Mountain's own west side, crosses a blasted-out cliff cut, loses a little elevation, then climbs again over Methow Pass. Keep going past Methow Pass and watch the right-hand (east) side of the trail: the spur is an unsigned use path that is easy to walk straight past.

waypoints.name: Snowy Lakes basin camp
waypoints.note: Established camping between Upper and Lower Snowy Lake; Lower Snowy Lake sits closest to Tower Mountain and is the usual base for the southwest route.
waypoints.directions: The spur climbs east off the PCT, gaining roughly 400 to 500 feet in about half a mile onto the bench holding the two lakes. Lower Snowy Lake is the one to camp at for this route; Upper Snowy sits higher and farther from the peak. Use the established sites, as the basin is heavily used and the meadow is thin.

waypoints.name: Headwall cave-ledge bypass
waypoints.note: A large headwall blocks direct access to the summit gully; climbers' path crosses talus/scree on the headwall's west side then follows an exposed-looking (but moderate) ledge past a 20-ft-tall cave mouth visible from Snowy Lakes to reach the gully entrance.
waypoints.directions: From Lower Snowy Lake make a rising traverse toward Tower's west face, crossing talus and scree, staying below the minor cliff bands and threading through or above the scrub to reach the main talus slope. Aim for the left (west) side of the headwall and climb scree up that flank to pick up the start of the ledge, which then cuts back right above the headwall to the cave. Pick the cave mouth out from camp before you start: it is visible from the lakes and is the one reliable landmark on an otherwise featureless slope.

waypoints.name: Main summit gully
waypoints.note: Class 3-4 gully above the cave ledge; right side has more ledges/holds and is usually cairned, center and left are steeper and more exposed.
waypoints.directions: Past the cave the ledge continues a short distance and delivers you to the foot of the gully. The step across looks more serious than it climbs and stays moderate. Helmets on from here, because anything a party above knocks loose funnels straight down the gully.

waypoints.name: Tower Mountain
waypoints.note: True summit; descend by reversing the gully and cave-ledge system back to the west-ridge notch rather than continuing over technical terrain.
waypoints.directions: Climb the gully on its right side, where the rock is more featured and the cairns are; the centre and left are steeper and more exposed. The rock is genuinely loose, so keep the party tight or well out of each other's fall line and move steadily. Follow the cairns out right toward the ridge crest and resist exiting early, since the exit is higher than it looks; one short exposed move gains the final ridge, which walks to the large summit cairn.

before.descent_text: Descend by reversing the ascent line — this is a walk-off/downclimb with no rappelling required (rappels: 0). From the summit, downclimb back through the broken rock to the ridge notch, then follow the ramp/ledge system down the climber's-right side of the main gully, retracing the zigzag line back past the cave and reddish boulder, and back across the talus field to the Snowy Lakes camp. The gully is the crux of the descent from a hazard standpoint: the rock is loose and rockfall is a real risk both from your own party and from any other parties on route, so descend it deliberately, one person at a time through constrictions, and keep helmets on until clear of the gully and talus. From Snowy Lakes, reverse the approach hike out via Methow Pass, Granite Pass, and Cutthroat Pass back to the Rainy Pass PCT trailhead; if Granite Pass still holds snow, downclimb it with the same care (ice axe) used on the way in.

itinerary.cal: Highway 20 (North Cascades Hwy) typically opens in May; the SW gully/talus can still hold snow into July, so most parties go July-September for driest, safest rock.

days.note: An easy, scenic backpack almost entirely on the Pacific Crest Trail from Rainy Pass, over Cutthroat Pass and Granite Pass, then a short side trip down into the Snowy Lakes basin to camp. Trail is well graded and mostly moderate grade; multiple trip reports clock this leg at roughly 5-6 hours with overnight packs.

schedule.label: Leave Rainy Pass trailhead
schedule.detail: PCT north; some parties start midday after driving up from Seattle.

schedule.label: Cutthroat Pass / Granite Pass
schedule.detail: First views of Tower Mountain and Golden Horn from the pass.

schedule.label: Arrive Snowy Lakes, make camp
schedule.detail: Upper Snowy Lake is preferred for views; Lower Snowy Lake camps are also common and closer to the Tower climber's path.

days.objective: Establish camp at Upper or Lower Snowy Lake

days.note: Leave camp with a light day pack for the summit push: cross talus below the west face (can hold snow early season), pass the large cave feature on the climber's path, then work up the loose class 3 gully with a short class 4 slab/exposed step near the top. After returning to camp, break it down and reverse the PCT back to the car — a long but standard single push for fit parties; some groups instead split this into two separate days if they want a more relaxed pace.
days.title: Climb Tower Mountain, then hike out

schedule.label: Leave camp for Tower Mountain
schedule.detail: Day pack, helmet on for the gully — rockfall is a real hazard, especially with parties above.

schedule.label: Reach the cave and gully entrance
schedule.detail: Notable ~25-yard-deep cave along the climber's path is a common landmark/rest stop.

schedule.label: Summit Tower Mountain
schedule.detail: Final moves are class 3-4 over blocks and a short chimney; loose rock throughout the gully.

schedule.label: Back at camp
schedule.detail: Break down tent and reload overnight pack.

schedule.label: Depart camp, hike out via PCT
schedule.detail: Reverse Granite Pass / Cutthroat Pass route back to Rainy Pass.

schedule.label: Arrive trailhead
schedule.detail: Some parties use a steeper Swamp Creek bushwhack shortcut to cut this leg short, at the cost of off-trail travel.

days.objective: Summit via the SW gully system and pack out to the trailhead

itinerary.totalNote: A 2-day, ~23-mile round trip with ~4,200 ft total gain: an easy PCT backpack in to Snowy Lakes camp, then a long summit-and-hike-out day on Tower's loose SW gully. Strong parties sometimes push the whole thing car-to-car in one very long day instead.
